Judgement in Appeal No.3 of 2019
J U D G M E N T
PER HON’BLE MR. AJAY TALEGAONKAR, TECHNICAL MEMBER
Background and Factual Matrix
1. The present appeal has been filed by the Municipal Corporation of Greater
Mumbai assailing the Order dated 05.11.2018 passed by the Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission (“CERC”/ “Respondent No. 1”) in Petition No.
159/MP/2017.
2. The Appellant is acting through its undertaking known as Brihanmumbai
Electric Supply and Transport Undertaking (“BEST”). BEST is a statutory
municipal undertaking and a distribution licensee which supplies electricity in
the Island City of Mumbai.
3. Respondent No. 1, CERC, is the statutory Commission constituted under
Section 76 of the Electricity Act, 2003. Respondent No. 2, TPTCL, is an inter-
State electricity trader and Respondent No. 3, Jindal India Thermal Power
Limited (“JITPL”), is a generating company operating a generating station at
Angul, Odisha.
4. To meet its anticipated power shortfall after availing its contracted capacity,
BEST invited expressions of interest in December 2015 for purchase of round-
the-clock and day power for the period from 01.02.2016 to 31.12.2016. The
bids were to be quoted month-wise at the delivery point, inclusive of all charges
and were to be submitted by 05.01.2016.
Page 3 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No.3 of 2019
5. Following the competitive process, BEST issued a Letter of Intent (“LoI”) dated
14.01.2016 to TPTCL for firm supply of power; 50 MW in March 2016 at ₹
2.95/kWh, 50 MW in April 2016 at ₹ 3.03/kWh, 30 MW in July 2016 at ₹
3.07/kWh, and 50 MW in December 2016 at ₹ 3.11/kWh. The stipulated
delivery point was the interface of the intra-State transmission network in
Maharashtra. The rates included TPTCL’s trading margin.
6. The LoI, inter alia, required BEST to pay correct bills within 30 days, provided
for a delayed-payment surcharge and a prompt-payment rebate, allocated
open-access charges and losses up to the delivery point to TPTCL and
required TPTCL to arrange alternative supply at the contracted tariff if the
generating source failed. It also contained compensation provisions for short
scheduling or drawal and a force-majeure clause which, among other events,
referred to a change in law and regulatory intervention.
7. By Notification dated 29.02.2016, the Ministry of Finance increased Clean
Energy Cess, later termed Clean Environment Cess, from ₹ 200 per tonne to
₹ 400 per tonne with effect from 00:00 hours of 01.03.2016. JITPL, by letter
dated 10.03.2016, requested TPTCL to accept an increase of ₹ 0.151/kWh in
the tariff on account of the enhanced cess.
8. TPTCL, by letter dated 11.03.2016, informed BEST of the increased cess and
sought acceptance of an additional ₹ 0.151/kWh, treating the increase as a
change in law under Clause 17 of the LoI. BEST, by e-mail dated 18.04.2016,
declined the request, stating that the LoI did not provide for compensatory tariff
on account of a revision in taxes, duties or cess and that the accepted bid price
remained constant during the contractual period.
Page 4 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No.3 of 2019
9. JITPL reiterated its request to TPTCL on 23.04.2016. TPTCL reiterated its
request to BEST on 13.05.2016 and by letter dated 07.09.2016, forwarded a
legal opinion dated 12.08.2016 in support of its claim. BEST did not accept the
claim.
10. TPTCL thereafter forwarded a debit note dated 08.01.2017 for ₹ 1,34,97,683
towards the alleged increase in per-unit cost from 01.03.2016 to 31.07.2016.
BEST, by letter dated 08.02.2017, forwarded its legal opinion dated 23.01.2017
and reiterated that, in a short-term power-supply arrangement without a
change-in-law provision, the requested tariff increase could not be allowed.
11. TPTCL maintained its claim by letter dated 31.03.2017, relying on Clause 17(e)
of the LoI; BEST reiterated its refusal on 19.06.2017. TPTCL then sent a further
debit note dated 04.07.2017 for ₹ 46,90,253 towards the alleged increase for
01.12.2016 to 31.12.2016. BEST again declined the request by e-mail dated
11.07.2017, referring to its earlier communications.
12. CERC passed the Impugned Order dated 05.11.2018 in Petition No.
159/MP/2017 and held that TPTCL and JITPL are entitled to recover from
BEST the differential amount towards Clean Energy CESS in proportion to the
coal consumed corresponding to scheduled generation at normative
parameters as per applicable tariff regulations or actuals, whichever is lower.
13. Aggrieved from the above, the Appellant has filed the present Appeal.
14. The Appellant has prayed for the following relief from us:
“a) That this Hon’ble Tribunal be pleased (i) to set aside the Impugned
Order dated 05.11.2018 passed by the Respondent No.1 (i.e., CERC), in
Page 5 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No.3 of 2019
the Case No. 159/MP/2017 filed by the Respondent Nos. 2 & 3 (i.e.,
TPTCL & JITPL), and (ii) to dismiss the said Case No. 159/MP/2017.
b) That the Costs of this Appeal be provided for by this Hon’ble
Tribunal; and
c) For such further or other relief as circumstances and nature of the
case may require.”
Submissions of the Appellant
15. BEST submitted that CERC wrongly rejected its objection of absence of privity
with JITPL. The LoI was exclusively between BEST and TPTCL, a merchant
trader which assumed the commercial, financial and tax risks. Mere
identification of JITPL’s station as the source did not create a contract between
BEST and JITPL.
16. BEST emphasised that it had no agreement, correspondence or payment
arrangement with JITPL; payments were made only to TPTCL; JITPL
addressed its cess claims only to TPTCL in letters dated 10.03.2016 and
23.04.2016; and there was no documented agreement or disclosed back-to-
back arrangement between TPTCL and JITPL. Therefore, CERC’s finding that
JITPL supplied power to BEST through a back-to-back arrangement is
challenged.
17. BEST submitted that the precedents relied upon by CERC in the Impugned
Order concerned known and documented back-to-back agreements and are
distinguishable. It further contends that Clause 17(E) of the LoI, occurring in
the force-majeure clause, could not be converted into an independent change-
Page 6 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No.3 of 2019
in-law compensation clause by importing the standard/model PPA framework
under Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003 (EA).
18. According to BEST, the short-term firm purchase for four specified months was
neither under a formal PPA nor pursuant to Section 63; the LoI deliberately did
not allow tariff escalation. Reading a substantive change-in-law remedy into
Clause 17(E) would rewrite the LoI and defeat its purpose. In any event, any
relief under that clause could extend only to force-majeure consequences
contemplated by its terms.
19. BEST also challenged CERC’s reliance on Section 70 of the Indian Contract
Act, 1872. It submitted that Section 70 cannot displace an express contract, is
inapplicable where the claim is contractually envisaged, and requires a
voluntary option to accept a non-gratuitous benefit; an option BEST neither had
nor exercised. It relied on AIR 1960 SC 588, AIR 1962 SC 779, (2007) 13 SCC
544, AIR 1984 Gauhati 11, AIR 1957 Madras 169 and AIR 1938 Lahore 71.
20. The Ministry of Power’s Direction dated 27.08.2018 under Section 107 of the
Electricity Act is said to be inapplicable because it concerns PPAs executed
under Section 63, whereas the LoI was neither a Section 63 PPA nor issued
under the short-term procurement guidelines/ resolutions dated 15.05.2012 or
30.03.2016. BEST also noted that the TPTCL’s additional affidavit filed before
CERC dated 05.09.2018 recognized this Section 63 limitation.
21. Pending the final disposal of the present Appeal, BEST deposited ₹1,81,00,000
on 03.05.2023, ₹18,02,018 on 11.06.2023, and ₹1,80,80,019 on 18.12.2025
with TPTCL. It seeks refund of these amounts with appropriate interest.
Page 7 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No.3 of 2019
Submissions of the Respondent No. 2, TPTCL
22. TPTCL submitted that it falls within the category of traders with an identified
source and delivery point, unlike a merchant trader with neither. Clause 10 of
BEST’s EoI required disclosure and confirmation of the source; Clauses 2 and
3 of the LoI identified JITPL and the delivery point. BEST, having stipulated
and incorporated those requirements, cannot deny privity.
23. TPTCL accepted the LoI, supplied power from JITPL’s station, and BEST paid
for that power. The LoI and the parties’ conduct established an enforceable
contractual relationship between BEST, TPTCL and JITPL for the supply
period.
24. Though there was no separate PPA between TPTCL and JITPL, JITPL
authorised TPTCL to supply power on a back-to-back basis. Privity may arise
from express or implied conduct. BEST’s plea of no privity is said to defeat the
Respondents’ legitimate claim, although JITPL bore the increased coal-related
cess as the disclosed generator.
25. Clause 17(E) of LoI must be purposively construed on restitution principles so
that the change-in-law covenant is not rendered meaningless. CERC’s
reference to the standard model PPA under Section 63, TPTCL submitted, did
not rewrite the LoI; it was within CERC’s regulatory jurisdiction and served the
commercial bargain.
26. The LoI was unilaterally drafted and issued by BEST without consultation with
TPTCL or JITPL. Therefore, under the doctrine of contra proferentem, BEST
cannot rely on the wording or form of Clause 17(E) to avoid liability. TPTCL
relied on United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Pushpalaya Printers, (2004) 3 SCC
Page 8 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No.3 of 2019
694; wherein it was held that “Where the words of a document are ambiguous,
they shall be construed against the party who prepared the document.” This
rule of construction was reiterated by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in its
judgment dated 25.04.2022 passed in Civil Appeal No. 4139 of 2020, Haris
Marine Products v. Export Credit Guarantee Corporation (ECGC) Limited,
wherein it was held that the rule of contra proferentem protects the insured
from the vagaries of an unfavorable interpretation of an ambiguous term to
which it did not agree. Further referred to the judgment dated 13.04.2018
passed by this Hon’ble Tribunal in Appeal No. 210 of 2017, Adani Power Ltd.
v. CERC & Ors., wherein the said principle of contra proferentem was similarly
invoked in the context of a Change in Law dispute under a power purchase
agreement.
27. TPTCL further relied on GMR Warora Energy Ltd. v. CERC, Appeal No. 111 of
2017, decided on 14.08.2018, where increases in excise duty, Clean Energy
Cess, service tax and Swachh Bharat Cess were held to be change-in-law
events. It therefore contended that the increased Clean Energy Cess is
compensable under the LoI.
Submissions of the Respondent No. 3, JITPL
28. JITPL submitted that BEST’s plea that it was a stranger to the transaction
contradicts the EoI and the parties’ conduct. Clause 10 of BEST’s December
2015 EoI required the bidder to identify and obtain confirmation from the source
of supply; TPTCL accordingly identified JITPL’s station, which BEST expressly
recorded as the source in the LoI.
29. TPTCL was therefore not a merchant trader free to purchase power from any
market source, but an intermediary procuring JITPL’s identified power for
Page 9 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No.3 of 2019
onward supply to BEST. JITPL authorised the supply, BEST accepted it and
made payment; the arrangement was acted upon by all three parties.
30. The absence of direct correspondence or payments between BEST and JITPL
does not negate the commercial nexus. The LoI identified the source, quantum,
period and consideration; BEST accepted TPTCL’s offer and acted upon the
transaction. JITPL submitted that these facts establish an enforceable
contractual relationship, consistent with the principle that non-signatories may
be bound in a back-to-back arrangement having a direct nexus.
31. Short-term procurement is, according to JITPL, within the regulatory
framework. BEST’s procurement through short-term bilateral purchase for
February-December 2016 was recorded and approved in MERC’s Multi-Year
Tariff Order dated 28.10.2016 in Case No. 33 of 2016. Regulations 18 and 19
of the MERC MYT Regulations, 2015 recognise long-term, medium-term and
short-term procurement under the approved power-procurement plan. BEST
itself described the procurement as competitive bidding in its reply dated
05.10.2017.
32. JITPL submitted that Clause 17(E) expressly uses the term “Change in Law.”
Since the EoI/ LoI were framed by BEST, they must be construed to give the
expression effect; the doctrine of contra proferentem operates against BEST.
The LoI contains no stipulation excluding financial relief for a change-in-law
event.
33. The Ministry of Power’s direction dated 27.08.2018 under Section 107 required
pass-through under Change in Law of changes in domestic duties, levies, cess
and taxes imposed by the Central/State Governments or Governmental
Page 10 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No.3 of 2019
Instrumentalities resulting in a corresponding change in cost.; it does not
distinguish short-term and long-term arrangements. JITPL/ TPTCL placed it
before CERC by additional affidavit dated 05.09.2018, to which BEST replied
on 22.10.2018. The direction reflects Clause 6.2.4 of the Tariff Policy dated
28.01.2016, issued under Section 3 of the Electricity Act.
34. CERC’s reference to the standard/model PPA did not rewrite the LoI; it
supplied recognised requirements for an expressly used but undefined term.
The notification dated 29.02.2016, which increased Clean Energy Cess from
₹200/MT to ₹400/MT, occurred after the relevant cut-off date and directly
increased the cost of generation and supply; hence it was rightly treated as a
change-in-law event.
35. JITPL submitted that “firm basis” in the LoI meant firm supply from JITPL’s
identified source during the stipulated time block under the LoI. Contract
duration is immaterial where a statutory change affects a variable component
such as coal cost.
36. BEST received the benefit of firm supply despite the additional statutory
expenditure incurred by JITPL/ TPTCL. Section 70 prevents retention of the
benefit of a non-gratuitous act without corresponding compensation. Reliance
was placed on Wardha Power Company Ltd. v. Reliance Infrastructure Ltd. &
Ors., Appeal No. 288 of 2014, decided on 12.09.2014, to submit that CERC
need not revisit the bidder’s assumed costs while granting change-in-law relief.
37. JITPL submitted that the impugned order is reasoned, based on the EoI, LoI,
conduct of parties and settled change-in-law principles and therefore seeks
Page 11 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No.3 of 2019
dismissal of the appeal and affirmation of the order dated 05.11.2018 with
corrigendum dated 03.12.2018.
Our Analysis and Conclusions
38. We have heard the Learned Counsel for the Appellant and the Learned
Counsel for the Respondents at length. We have also carefully considered their
respective submissions and the relevant material on record. Upon due
consideration of the arguments advanced and the documents placed before
us, we now proceed to analyse the issues arising for our consideration in the
present Appeal.
39. We consider it relevant to take note of the fact that the conduct of JITPL and
TPTCL following the increase in the rate of Clean Energy Cess. The Ministry
of Finance, Government of India, vide Notification dated 29.02.2016 increased
the Clean Energy Cess from ₹ 200 per MT to ₹ 400 per MT with effect from
01.03.2016. Thereafter, JITPL, by its letter dated 10.03.2016, requested
TPTCL to accept an increase of ₹ 0.151/kWh in the tariff on account of the
enhanced cess which was communicated by TPTCL to BEST vide letter dated
11.03.2016. BEST, however, by its e-mail dated 18.04.2016, declined the
request, stating that the LoI did not provide for any compensatory tariff on
account of revision in taxes, duties or cess and that the accepted bid price was
to remain constant throughout the contractual period.
40. JITPL reiterated its claim by letter dated 23.04.2016, followed by TPTCL’s letter
dated 13.05.2016. Thereafter, TPTCL also obtained a legal opinion dated
12.08.2016 in support of its claim which was forwarded to BEST on
07.09.2016. It is also noted that during this period, the parties continued to act
upon the original LoI. The supplies scheduled under the LoI for March, April
Page 12 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No.3 of 2019
and July 2016 were duly undertaken. TPTCL also continued to supply power
to BEST during December 2016 in terms of the original LoI at the tariff
stipulated therein. The aforesaid sequence of events makes an indication that
disagreement between the parties regarding the claim arising out of the
enhanced cess continued. The implications, if any, of such conduct for the
parties’ respective rights and obligations would have to be considered in the
context of the terms of the LoI and the issues arising for our consideration.
41. We note that the core submissions of BEST are twofold. First being that it had
no privity of the contract or arrangement that TPTCL had with generating
company JITPL, and second being that the change in law (CIL) provision was
mentioned as one of the conditions leading to Force Majeure (FM), and
therefore was not meant for economic restitution. These submissions were
made by BEST before CERC also.
42. In the Impugned Order, after analysing the facts of the case, CERC had
rejected the contention of BEST that it had no privity of contract between
TPTCL and JITPL. Thereafter, CERC allowed economic restitution under
Section 70 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. We deem it appropriate to first
address the second aspect, namely, whether economic restitution is
permissible in the facts and circumstances of the case. It is admitted position
that CIL was mentioned as part of FM in the tender document as well as LoI
issued by BEST. The S. No. 17 of the terms and conditions of the supply, as
extracted from the LoI is reproduced below:
“17.Force majeure- A Force Majeure event or circumstance or combination
of events or circumstances (not otherwise constituting and Indian political
event) that adversely affects, prevents or delays any party in the
performance of its obligation in accordance with the terms of this agreement,
but only if and to the extent that (i) such events and circumstances are not
Page 13 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No.3 of 2019
within the reasonable control of the affected party, and (ii) such events or
circumstances could not have been prevented through employment of
prudent utility practices. Neither party shall be in breach of its obligations
pursuant to this understanding to the extent that the performance of its
obligation was prevented, hindered or delayed due to force majeure event,
and without in any way prejudicing the obligation of either party to make
payments of amounts accrued due prior to the occurrence of the event of
force majeure, which shall be payable on the original due date. Force
majeure events shall include but not limited to:
A) Act of war, invasion, armed conflict, blockade, revolution, riot, resurrection
or civil commotion, terrorism, sabotage, fire explosion or criminal damage;
B) Act of God, including fire, lighting, cyclone, typhoon, flood, tidal wave,
storm, earthquake, landslide, epidemic or similar cataclysmic event;
C) Any curtailment/ suspension / non availability of transmission capacity by
intervening SLDC’s / RLDC’s;
D) Any restriction imposed by any RLDC’s and including generation
constraints/ equipment breakdown/ islanding/ accidents;
E) Change in law;
F) Regulatory intervention in the matter of power trading as also orders from
CERC/ SERCs/ Appellate Tribunal of Electricity/ High Courts/ Supreme
Court particularly related to rates at which power can be sold/ purchased/
traded. This will also include regulations, orders already issued buy yet to be
conclusively enforced.
G) Any directive by Government of Maharashtra not to export / import power
outside Maharashtra boundary.”
43. A careful perusal of the LoI indicates that the above extracted provision is the
only provision therein which refers to CIL. Consistent with conventional
practice, the FM clause in the present case is concerned with events which
affect a party’s ability to perform its contractual obligations and appears to
provide for relief from the consequences of delay or non-performance arising
therefrom. The provision in question contains a non-exhaustive list of events
which may give rise to such circumstances, and CIL finds mention amongst
those events. It is, therefore, evident that the reference to CIL was intended to
cover situations where, owing to a change in law, a party is prevented from or
is unable to perform its contractual obligations, thereby attracting the FM
Page 14 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No.3 of 2019
provision1. The reference to CIL in this context is thus intended to provide relief
in respect of delay or non-performance and cannot be construed as an
independent provision for economic restitution on account of the financial
impact of a change in law. We, therefore, agree with the contention of BEST
that the reference to CIL in the LoI is in the context of FM and is not intended
to provide for economic restitution.
44. We find that paragraphs 32 and 33 of the Impugned Order are crucial to
understand analysis of CERC on this issue. For the sake of convenience, the
aforesaid paragraphs of the Impugned Order are extracted below:
“32. The submissions have been considered. It is evident from clause 17 of
LoI as quoted in para30 above that “force majeure” can be invoked where
“any event or circumstances or combination of events or circumstances
adversely affects, prevents or delays any party in the performance of its
obligations”.Further, Clause 17 provides an inclusive definition of Force
Majeure. Clause 17(E) recognises “change in law”as an event of force
majeure. Unlike in the case of standard PPAs, Change in Law in Clause
17(E) is neither defined nor has its scope been clearly delineated. In our
view, an event would constitute a change in law, even though it may not
qualify as a force majeure in terms of the LoI, if it meets the requirements
of change in law in standard PPA. In the standard model PPA issued by
Ministry of Power Government of India under Section 63 of the 2003 Act,
the term “Law” inter alia includes any statute, ordinance, regulation,
notification or code, rule or any interpretation of any of them by an Indian
Governmental Instrumentality and having force of law. The term „Change in
Law‟ includes any enactment, bringing into effect, adoption, promulgation,
amendment, modification or repeal of any law, occurrence of any of the
events mentioned therein if the same has occurred after the cut-off date
(which is seven days before the bid deadline) and has the effect of incurring
1 A CIL event may, in certain circumstances, go beyond merely increasing the cost of
performance and actually prevent performance of contractual obligations. For instance,
changes in environmental requirements may result in statutory directions prohibiting
operation of a generating station until the prescribed requirements are met. This was
illustrated in the case of Stage-II of Badarpur Thermal Power Station, which was
directed to be shut down by the Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC) in November
2016 in view of environmental concerns. Consequently, the generating units, though
otherwise capable of operating, were prevented from generating electricity.
Page 15 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No.3 of 2019
of recurring or non-recurring expenditure by the Seller (Generating
Company). In the present case, the Petitionershave claimed compensation
for additional expenditure incurred by Petitioner No.1 due to increase rate
of Clean Energy Cess on coal,after the cut-off date (31.12.2015) based on
MOF, GOI notification dated 29.2.2016. Thus, the increase in levy of Clean
Energy Cess, in our view, qualifies as a „change in law‟ event in terms of
clause 17(E) of the LoI. It is pertinent to note that the Model PPA provides
for the award of compensation for Change in Law which occurred during the
Construction Period and Operating Period. In the absence of any such
provision for award of compensation for change in law in the LoI, it needs
to be considered as to what relief should be admissible for Change in Law
on account of change in rate of Clean Energy Cess.
33. The Petitioners have submitted that the increase in levy of Clean Energy
Cess qualifies as a change in law event under clause 17 of the LoI and
hence they ought to be compensated in terms of clause 17 and restored
back to the same economic position as if such change in law has not
occurred.It is to be noted that compensations under a contract has to be
governed as per the provisions of the contract. The LoI dated 14.1.2016
does not contain any provision for payment of compensation on the
occurrence of events of change in law. Further, Change in Law has been
shown under “force majeure”. The compensation for force majeure under
the LoI is in terms of the following:
“Neither party shall be in breach of its obligations pursuant to this
understanding to the extent that the performance of its obligation was
prevented, hindered or delayed due to force majeure event, and
without in any way prejudicing the obligation of either party to make
payments of amounts accrued due prior to the occurrence of the event
of force majeure, which shall be payable on the original due date.”
Since “Change in Law” is a sub-sect of force majeure, the above provisions
will be applicable for Change in Law also. In terms of the above provision,
neither party will be in breach of its obligations to the extent the performance
of its obligation was prevented or hindered or delayed due to force majeure
event. Change in rates of Clean Energy Cess which is covered under
Change in Law and is a force majeure event in terms of the LoI will certainly
hinder JITPL/TPTCL from discharging their obligations under the LoI and
for such hindrance, JITPL/TPTCL would not have been in breach of their
obligation under the LoI. However, JITPL/TPTCL despite being affected by
force majeure arising out of change in law have supplied power by incurring
additional expenditure. In our view, JITPL/TPTCL needs to be considered
for compensation for the additional expenditure incurred by them on
account of change in rate of Clean Energy Cess on coal which was used
for supply of power to BEST.”
Page 16 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No.3 of 2019
45. It may be seen that, in paragraph 32, the CERC has examined whether the
increase in the rate of Clean Energy Cess constitutes CIL. In the absence of
any definition of CIL in the tender document or the LoI, the CERC has relied
upon the relevant provisions of the Model PPA issued by the Government of
India under Section 63 of the Act and concluded that an increase in the rate of
Clean Energy Cess is covered under CIL. We do not find any error in the
analysis of the CERC up to this point. However, we find it difficult to appreciate
that, in the latter part of the same paragraph, despite recognising that the LoI
contains no provision for grant of compensation on account of CIL, the CERC
proceeds to consider the relief that may be admissible on account of the
increase in the rate of Clean Energy Cess, without identifying any contractual
or regulatory basis for granting such relief.
46. In paragraph 33 of the Impugned Order, the CERC reiterates that CIL forms
part of FM under Clause 17 of the LoI, which relates to performance
obligations. However, in the latter part of the same paragraph, the CERC
proceeds on the premise that, even though JITPL/ TPTCL were affected and
hindered by FM arising from CIL, they had supplied power to BEST by incurring
additional expenditure and were, therefore, entitled to compensation. In our
opinion, the CERC has erred in proceeding on the assumption that, merely
because a change in the rate of Clean Energy Cess qualifies as CIL and CIL
is included amongst the events covered under the FM clause, the affected
parties would automatically become entitled to compensation for the resulting
increase in the cost of performance. What the CERC has failed to appreciate
is that the FM provision in the LoI is concerned with performance obligations
and provides relief in the event of delay or non-performance arising from the
Page 17 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No.3 of 2019
specified events. It does not provide for economic restitution on account of an
increase in the cost of performing contractual obligations.
47. TPTCL contended that confining Clause 17(E) of LoI to force majeure would
render the reference to change in law otiose. We do not agree. A change in
law which satisfies the conditions of Clause 17 attracts the protection against
delay in performance or non-performance as expressly provided therein.
48. The contention based on contra proferentem must be examined by reading the
LoI as a whole. Upon doing so, we find no ambiguity concerning the relief
provided by Clause 17, and therefore the question of construing any ambiguity
against BEST does not arise. In our view, Clause 17 specifies protection
against breach arising from affected performance; it does not stipulate
adjustment of the agreed consideration. The absence of an express prohibition
against reimbursement of increased cost does not, by itself, create an
entitlement to reimbursement.
49. JITPL also seek to sustain the compensation awarded by CERC by relying
upon the MoP’s direction dated 27.08.2018. Although the Impugned Order
records this submission, it does not determine the applicability of the direction.
We have, therefore, independently considered this contention. The direction,
read with Clause 6.2(4) of the Tariff Policy, 2016, favours pass-through of
increased statutory levies unless otherwise provided in the PPA.
50. The relevant extract of the MoP letter dated 27.08.2018 is extracted below:
“ Para 6.2 (4) of Tariff Policy 2016 provides that after the award of
bids, if there is any change in domestic duties, levies, cess and taxes
imposed by Central Government, State Governments/Union Territories or
by any Government instrumentality leading to corresponding changes in

the cost, the same may be treated as “Change in Law” and may unless
provided otherwise in the PPA, be allowed as pass through subject to
approval of Appropriate Commission.
2. It has been brought to the notice of this Ministry that Generating
Companies are facing difficulties in getting pass-through of changes in
cost due to any change in domestic duties, levies, cess and taxes imposed
by Central Government, State Governments/Union Territories or by any

in the Power Sector.
3. Now, in order to address the above issue and ensure sustainability
of the electricity market in the larger public interest, the Central
Government, in exercise of the powers conferred under section 107 of the

or by any Government instrumentality leading to corresponding

51. It may be seen that paragraph 2 of the MoP’s letter identifies the problem it
seeks to address namely the considerable time taken by the Appropriate
Commission to approve the pass-through of changes in domestic duties,
levies, cess and taxes, which has caused cash flow difficulties for generating
companies. Paragraph 3(a) then provides that the resulting change in cost may
be treated as “Change in Law” and may, “unless provided otherwise in the
PPA”, be allowed as a pass-through.
52. Read together, these paragraphs show that the letter is directed at expediting
relief, not at creating a new entitlement. The expression “Change in Law”,
placed within double quotation marks, is used as a defined term. It refers to a
Page 19 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No.3 of 2019
Change in Law provision (clause or article) that already exists in the PPA and
addresses the consequences of such change. Where a PPA contains no such
provision, there is no contractual mechanism for economic restitution on
account of Change in Law. To read the letter as creating that entitlement would
be to import into the PPA a term the parties did not agree to, contrary to the
contractual arrangement. The qualifier “unless provided otherwise in the PPA”
reinforces this; the direction operates within the four corners of the PPA and
does not override it. Accordingly, the intent of the letter cannot be to insert a
Change in Law provision into a contract that does not contain one.
53. In Fatehgarh Bhadla Transmission Company Limited v. Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission & Ors., Appeal No. 352 of 2022, decided on
02.05.2023, this Tribunal explained that Section 107(1) requires the Central
Commission to be guided by written directions of the Central Government on
matters of policy involving public interest. Such directions are to be taken into
consideration by the Commission while discharging its functions and it is not
bound by such guidance. Further, in Kerala State Electricity Board Ltd. v.
Jhabua Power Ltd. & Ors., 2024 INSC 768, the Hon’ble Supreme Court held
that a policy direction under Section 108 of the Electricity Act, 2003 cannot
displace the adjudicatory function entrusted to the State Commission. Section
107(1) uses the same expression, “shall be guided by”, in relation to directions
issued by the Central Government to the Central Commission. The same
reasoning therefore applies to the Ministry of Power’s direction dated
27.08.2018. Accordingly, the Ministry’s direction could, at most, guide the
Central Commission in dealing with an admissible pass-through claim. It could
not confer on JITPL or TPTCL a right to recover the additional cess from BEST
where there is no express provision for economic restitution.

54. Our analysis in the preceding paragraph is consistent with Gujarat Urja Vikas
Nigam Ltd. v. Solar Semiconductor Power Co. (India) (P) Ltd., (2017) 16
SCC 498, where the Hon’ble Supreme Court explained that the Commission
cannot invoke its inherent powers to vary the terms of a PPA, and that those
terms bind both parties. If the Commission cannot alter the agreed terms
through its own powers, a policy direction that merely guides the Commission
cannot do so either. The direction dated 27.08.2018 therefore cannot be relied
upon to recover the differential cess from BEST over and above the rates
agreed in the LoI.
55. TPTCL has relied on this Tribunal’s judgment in GMR Warora Energy Ltd. v.
Central Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors., Appeal Nos. 111 and
290 of 2017, decided on 14.08.2018. In that case, this Tribunal upheld
compensation for the impact of Clean Energy Cess under Article 10 of the
respective PPAs, which expressly provided for economic restitution under
Change in Law provision. The decision supports the classification of the
increase in Clean Energy Cess as a Change in Law event. Entitlement to
recover the resulting additional cost from BEST, however, must be determined
under the terms of the LoI. Clause 17(E) refers to Change in Law only as an
event of Force Majeure and the LoI contains no provision for tariff adjustment
or compensation on that account. Accordingly, GMR Warora does not assist
TPTCL in its claim for recovery of the differential cess from BEST.
56. There is no doubt that the increase in the rate of Clean Energy Cess increased
the cost incurred by JITPL/ TPTCL in performing their contractual obligations
to BEST. However, an increase in the cost of performance does not, by itself,
amount to a hindrance to performance as concluded by the CERC, nor does it
Page 21 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No.3 of 2019
render the performance of contractual obligations impossible. The fact that the
affected parties continued to supply power, albeit at an increased cost, does
not establish that their ability to perform the contractual obligations was
hindered within the meaning of the FM provision. In the absence of any
contractual provision providing for economic restitution on account of CIL, the
mere inclusion of CIL amongst the events covered under the FM clause cannot
be construed as conferring an independent right to compensation for the
increased cost of performance.
57. It is well settled that an increase in the cost of performance of a contractual
obligation, by itself, does not constitute a Force Majeure event. In Energy
Watchdog v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors., (2017) 14
SCC 80, the Hon'ble Supreme Court, while considering the impact of an
unprecedented increase in the price of imported coal, held that the availability
of alternative modes of performance, albeit at a higher cost, would not frustrate
the contract. The Court reiterated the principle laid down in Alopi Parshad &
Sons Ltd. v. Union of India, 1960 SCC OnLine SC 13, that a party cannot be
absolved from its contractual obligations merely because performance has
become onerous on account of an unforeseen change in circumstances.
58. Having concluded that JITPL/ TPTCL is entitled to compensation for the
additional cost, the CERC invoked Section 70 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872,
to address what it characterised as an eventuality not contemplated under the
contract. The said Section 70 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 is reproduced
below for the sake of completeness:
“70. Obligation of person enjoying benefit of non-gratuitous act.—
Where a person lawfully does anything for another person, or delivers
anything to him, not intending to do so gratuitously, and such other person
Page 22 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No.3 of 2019
enjoys the benefit thereof, the latter is bound to make compensation to the
former in respect of, or to restore, the thing so done or delivered.”
59. Section 70 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 cannot be invoked to enhance the
agreed consideration for performance of an obligation already governed by a
subsisting contract. (Food Corporation of India v. Vikas Majdoor Kamdar
Sahkari Mandli Ltd., (2007) 13 SCC 544). Section 70 is a restitutionary
remedy applicable where a person lawfully does something for another, without
intending to act gratuitously, and the other party voluntarily accepts and enjoys
the benefit thereof (State of West Bengal v. B.K. Mondal & Sons, AIR 1962
SC 779). It may, therefore, support a claim for compensation for additional work
performed outside the agreed contractual scope, for which no consideration
was stipulated (V.R. Subramanyam v. B. Thayappa, AIR 1966 SC 1034).
Thus, an increase in the cost of performing an existing contractual obligation,
without more, does not give rise to a claim under Section 70.
60. In the present case, the supply of electricity by JITPL/ TPTCL to BEST was
pursuant to the subsisting contractual arrangement, which also stipulated the
consideration payable for such supply. The increase in the rate of Clean
Energy Cess resulted in an increase in the cost incurred by JITPL/TPTCL in
performing their existing contractual obligations. It did not involve any
additional work or supply of goods or services beyond the scope of the
contract, nor did it confer any additional benefit upon the BEST outside the
contractual arrangement. The mere fact that the BEST continued to receive the
benefit of electricity supplied under the contract, while the JITPL/ TPTCL
incurred an increased cost in supplying the same, cannot be treated as a non-
gratuitous act outside the contractual arrangement so as to attract Section 70.
To hold otherwise would effectively permit JITPL/ TPTCL to claim additional

consideration for performance of contractual obligations, notwithstanding the
consideration stipulated under the contract.
61. In view of the foregoing discussion, we conclude that neither any provision of
the contractual arrangement nor Section 70 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872,
comes to the aid of JITPL/ TPTCL to claim compensation for the enhanced
cost of generation due to an increase in Clean Energy Cess. Therefore, it is
unnecessary for us to get into the issue of whether or not BEST had privity of
contract between JITPL and TPTCL. Accordingly, the Impugned Order is liable
to be set aside.
62. BEST has deposited the amount with TPTCL towards the liability arising from
the Impugned Order. Since we have decided to set aside the Impugned Order,
the principle of restitution requires that BEST be restored, so far as money can
do so, to the position it would have occupied had the amounts not been
deposited. The refund must therefore include reasonable interest for the period
during which BEST was deprived of the use of those amounts. Therefore, we
consider it appropriate to award simple interest at the one-year Marginal Cost
of Funds Based Lending Rate (MCLR) of the State Bank of India, as applicable
from time to time, on each deposit from its respective date until the date of
actual refund.
